title: Week 8 - Disks
content: - Data stored as **magnetic orientation** on a spinning platter - A **mechanical arm** moves to the right location - Each side of a platter is called a surface - Each surface is organized into tracks - Tracks organized into sectors Disk service time is broken down into: - Seek - Rotational latency - Data transfer HDD friendly workloads have: - High locality - Large request sizes We try to design file systems so workloads they generate have those properties. # Disk Storage Disks expose storage as linear array of blocks. - Each block is 512 bytes or 4 KB - Number of blocks is disk capacity / block size Disk tries to map blocks close in LBN space to physical disk locations that are close to each other. ## Complications ### Zones In an HDD, the disk surface is divided into concentric tracks, and those tracks are grouped into zones. Zones are a complication because they introduce non-uniform physical layout and performance, even though the disk presents a simple linear block interface. ### Defect Management Disks keep spare sectors that are used in case portions of the media become unusable. ### Skew A request spans 2 tracks. The track skew can prevent unnecessary rotation. ## Scheduling **Seeks are expensive**, unless there are request queues disk scheduling has minimal impact. Modern disks do the scheduling themselves. - FCFS (do nothing) - Reasonable when load is low - Long waiting times for long request queues - SSTF (shortest seek time first) - Minimize arm movement (seek time), maximize request rate - Favors middle blocks/tracks - SCAN (elevator) - Service requests in one direction until done, then reverse - C-SCAN - Like SCAN, but only go in one direction (typewriter) - LOOK / C-LOOK - Like SCAN/C-SCAN but only go as far as last request in each direction (not full width of the disk)
